# The Art of Becoming: A Meditation on Change, Time, and the Selves We Carry

---

There is a photograph of me somewhere in my parents' house—I know this because every few years, when visiting home, I stumble upon it again. I am perhaps four years old, standing at the edge of a small pond in a public park, staring at my own reflection with an expression of absolute astonishment. My mouth is slightly open. My hands are pressed against my knees as I lean forward, as though I have just discovered something impossible, something that demands closer inspection.

That child and I share the same face, the same name, the same thread of continuity that we call a life. And yet, I could not tell you with any certainty that we share the same mind, the same way of seeing, the same fundamental way of being in the world. He was astonished by reflections. I am astonished, these days, by the persistence of that astonishment—by the fact that something in me still believes the world is capable of revealing itself in unexpected ways.

This is the paradox of becoming: we are never the same person twice, and yet we carry every version of ourselves with us, like nested dolls that somehow all remain conscious at once.

---

I have been thinking about change lately—not dramatic, cinematic change, not the kind that makes for compelling narratives about reinvention or redemption, but the quiet, almost imperceptible kind. The way a person's voice shifts over a decade without them noticing. The way preferences evolve so gradually that one day you find yourself enjoying a flavor you once found repulsive, and you cannot identify the exact moment your taste changed. The way certain friendships deepen while others dissolve, not from any single rupture, but from a slow drift, like two boats on a river that gradually find themselves carried by different currents.

This kind of change is difficult to write about precisely because it resists narrative. Stories demand events, turning points, moments of crisis or clarity. But the changes that most profoundly shape us are often invisible from the outside. They happen in the accumulation of unremarkable days—in the conversations that don't seem important at the time, in the books we read on ordinary afternoons, in the small decisions we make without realizing they are decisions at all.

I sometimes imagine a graph of a single human life, plotted not in years or milestones, but in moments of genuine transformation—moments when something shifted at a fundamental level, when the person who existed before the moment could not fully comprehend the person who existed after. If such a graph existed, I suspect it would be startling. The peaks and valleys would not align with the events we consider significant. The most dramatic turns might correspond to nothing more than a sentence someone said in passing, a dream that dissolved upon waking but left an emotional residue, an image glimpsed through a window at exactly the right moment.

What would it mean to see such a map of oneself? Would we recognize the person we've become?

---

There is a concept in philosophy called the Ship of Theseus, and it goes something like this: if you replace every plank of a ship, one by one, over the course of many years, is it still the same ship? The question has been debated for centuries, and I don't intend to resolve it here. But what interests me is not the ship itself—it's the experience of being the ship. Because this is what it feels like to be alive: to be perpetually under construction, to have parts of yourself replaced so gradually that you never notice the moment of substitution, and yet to feel, in some persistent way, that you are still you.

I remember being sixteen and convinced that my understanding of love was complete. I had read the poetry, watched the films, experienced the first infatuations that seemed to contain all the intensity of the universe compressed into a single glance. I felt I had grasped something essential. Now, looking back, I can see that my sixteen-year-old understanding of love was not wrong exactly, but it was... one-dimensional. It was a photograph of something that was actually in motion. I could see the colors, the shapes, the basic composition, but I could not see how it breathed, how it moved through time, how it could be both sustaining and terrifying, both simple and incomprehensibly complex.

And I know—with a certainty that feels like standing at the edge of something vast—that my current understanding, too, is incomplete. That there are dimensions of love I cannot yet perceive, that the forty-year-old version of me (if I am fortunate enough to become that person) will look back at my present understanding with the same gentle condescension I feel toward my younger self.

This is not a depressing thought. Or rather, it doesn't have to be. It can also be understood as a promise: that there is always more to discover, that the territory of human experience is inexhaustible, that we will never arrive at a final understanding because the landscape keeps shifting.

---

I think about the relationship between time and identity a great deal. We tend to think of ourselves as continuous beings, as the same person moving through the years, accumulating experiences the way a tree accumulates rings. But this metaphor, while comforting, may be misleading. A tree's rings are passive records—they do not influence each other, they do not revise or reinterpret each other. Human memory, by contrast, is constantly being rewritten. Each time we recall an event, we alter it slightly, layering present understanding onto past experience, until the memory becomes as much a record of who we are now as of who we were then.

This means that our past is not fixed. It exists in a state of perpetual revision, shaped by the person doing the remembering. The events themselves are gone—they exist only as neural patterns, as stories we tell ourselves—but the stories keep changing. In a very real sense, we are the authors of our own histories, and we are never finished writing.

I find this both liberating and unsettling. Liberating because it means we are not prisoners of our past—we can, to some extent, change the meaning of what happened to us by changing the way we understand it. The painful experiences of youth can be reframed as lessons, as catalysts, as necessary passages toward wisdom. The humiliations and failures can be understood not as evidence of inadequacy but as moments of growth that were, at the time, indistinguishable from suffering.

But it is unsettling because it means we can never be certain that our understanding of ourselves is accurate. If memory is mutable, if identity is a story we tell rather than a thing we possess, then how much of what we believe about ourselves is true? And what does "true" even mean in this context?

I don't have answers to these questions. I'm not sure answers exist. But I have found, over the years, that sitting with uncertainty is itself a form of wisdom. Not all questions need to be resolved. Some need only be inhabited.

---

There is a Japanese concept called "mono no aware"—sometimes translated as "the pathos of things" or "a sensitivity to ephemera." It refers to the bittersweet awareness that everything is passing, that beauty and sadness are intertwined, that the cherry blossoms are most beautiful precisely because they will fall. It is not a philosophy of despair but one of heightened attention—a way of seeing the world that acknowledges loss without being paralyzed by it.

I think this concept is closely related to the experience of becoming. To be in the process of changing is to be aware, on some level, that each version of yourself is temporary. The person reading these words is not the same person who began reading them—not in any meaningful neurological sense. Synapses have fired, patterns have shifted, new connections have formed or old ones have been reinforced. You are slightly different now than you were a few minutes ago.

This is not cause for alarm. It is simply what it means to be alive in a body, in a mind, in a world that does not stand still. The alternative to becoming is not stability—it is stasis, which is another word for death. The only way to remain the same is to stop processing new information, to stop adapting, to stop responding to the ceaseless flow of experience that constitutes a human life. And that, of course, is not really an option for the living.

So we change. We change constantly, in ways we notice and ways we don't, in ways we welcome and ways we resist. We become new versions of ourselves while insisting, sometimes desperately, that we are the same. And this insistence is not a lie—it is an act of faith, a recognition that continuity is not the same as sameness, that a river can flow and still be called by the same name, that a flame can persist while consuming entirely new fuel.

---

I think about the people in my life and the ways they have become themselves. My mother, who was once a shy girl in a small town and is now a woman of formidable presence, who navigates the world with a confidence that seems, from the outside, as natural and inevitable as gravity. But I know it was not always so. I know there were years of struggle, of self-doubt, of quiet decisions made in private that no one else witnessed. I know that the woman she is today was built, plank by plank, through countless moments of choosing who to be next.

My father, who carries within him a boy who loved mathematics and a young man who fell in love with literature and an older man who found peace in carpentry, all of these selves coexisting, not in conflict but in conversation. He is not three different people—he is one person who has allowed himself to grow in multiple directions, who has refused the pressure to be only one thing.

My friends, each of them carrying their own archives of becoming—paths taken and not taken, versions of themselves that exist now only in memory or in the stories they tell at dinner parties, embellished with time and perspective until the truth and the narrative have become indistinguishable.

And strangers—the people I pass on the street, each of them a universe of change, each of them in the middle of a transformation I will never see. The person rushing to catch a bus may be on their way to a conversation that will alter the course of their life. The person sitting alone on a bench may be in the process of letting go of something they have carried for years. We are all becoming, all the time, in ways that are invisible to each other and often invisible to ourselves.

---

I want to say something about resistance—about the ways we fight against our own becoming, the ways we cling to old versions of ourselves even when those versions no longer fit. There is a deep human impulse toward consistency, toward the belief that who we were determines who we must be. We build identities out of our histories and then defend them as though they were fortresses, as though the only alternative to being exactly who we have always been is to be no one at all.

But this is a false choice. We can honor our past without being enslaved by it. We can acknowledge the person we were while making room for the person we are becoming. This is not betrayal—it is growth. It is the natural and necessary work of a life that refuses to stand still.

I have known people who seemed trapped by their own narratives—people who could not forgive themselves for past mistakes, who could not see beyond the worst thing they had ever done, who believed with absolute conviction that they were defined by their failures. And I have watched, sometimes with awe, as those same people eventually found the courage to rewrite their stories—not to erase the past but to place it in a larger context, to see it as one chapter rather than the whole book.

This is, I think, one of the most profound acts of courage available to us: the willingness to let go of who we thought we were in order to become who we might be. It requires a tolerance for uncertainty, a comfort with ambiguity, a trust that the self is not a fixed point but a process, not a destination but a journey.

---

The child at the edge of the pond, staring at his own reflection—he did not know that he was looking at a self that would dissolve and reform countless times over the coming decades. He did not know that the face in the water would change, slowly and then suddenly, into something he would not recognize. He did not know that the astonishment he felt would become, years later, a kind of longing—a desire to see the world with that same freshness, that same sense of wonder at the simple fact of existence.

But here is what I want to believe: that the astonishment did not disappear. That it was not lost but transformed, carried forward in a different form into a different life. That somewhere in the architecture of my adult mind, there remains a small, persistent voice that still finds the world astonishing—not despite all the changes I've undergone but because of them. Because each transformation has revealed something new, something unexpected, something that demands the kind of close attention I first learned at the edge of that pond.

We are all standing at the edge of something. We are all leaning forward, hands pressed against our knees, staring into the depths of our own becoming. The reflection shifts. The water moves. The self we see is never quite the self we expected.

And that, I think, is the most astonishing thing of all.

---

*This piece is dedicated to all the selves I've been, and all the selves I have yet to become.*
